steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and the parts packed in the ash pan for shipping damage. The door and bypass handles ship inside the stove; fit them once it is in its final location.

• Pack list: stove, owner's manual, wood handles, screws and washers; Canadian Handle Kit 90-71310 where applicable.
  • Catalyst packing material stays in place and burns off during the first fire.
  • Handles: US installs mount directly on the stove (Illustration 1, p. 9). Canada: use the removable Canadian Handle Kit 90-71310; do not permanently install handles on the stove.
  • Lifting from underneath: temporarily remove the lower heat shield, and refit it once the stove is in position. It is required for safe operation.
  • The label hangs on a cable under the stove; don't damage it when lifting. After final positioning, store it in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
  • Freestanding room heater only. Not to be installed in any factory-built fireplace.
Floor protection
Combustible floors need a noncombustible protector under and beyond the stove: 37" x 31-1/2" minimum in the US, 47" x 41" in Canada. No insulated hearth pad is required.
Clearances to combustibles

Position the stove per the Figure 4 table for the connector type and rear heat shield (kit #90-68300) in use, and check the alcove limits. Trim and mantel clearances are in the Figure 6 drawing (p. 13).
Outside air (optional)
Kit #90-53300 connects the intake to a minimum 3" duct to the outside; terminate no higher than the stove's air intake, screened and hooded. Required in mobile homes.
Rear-exit conversion (if used)
To vent out the back, drop the rear 3/8" threaded rod, move the flue collar to the rear position, cap the top with the rear flue plate, then re-thread the rod into the cone nut.

1. Loosen (don't remove) the 3/8" nut under the stove with a 9/16" wrench, then turn the single rear 3/8" threaded rod out, reaching in through the flue collar with vise-grips or pliers.
  2. Remove the four bolts holding the top flue collar (7/16" wrench); don't drop bolts or washers into the stove.
  3. Through the top opening, remove the top two bolts and washers holding the rear flue plate.
  4. Loosen the bottom two bolts until the rear flue plate is free; remove the plate, leaving those two bolts in place.
  5. Hold the bottom two bolts and position the flue collar in the rear exit position; hand-tighten slightly.
  6. Insert the top two bolts with washers and fully tighten all four.
  7. Fold a paper towel to about 1-1/2" x 1-1/2" and set it on the cone nut to hold it in place. Place the flue plate on the top and tighten its four bolts (7/16").
  8. Under the stove, back the nut off 3 full turns, lift the rod, line it up with the cone nut and thread it in (about 5 full turns) through the rear flue collar. Tighten the 3/8" nut from step 1 with the 9/16" wrench.
Chimney connector
6" single wall 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel (never aluminum or galvanized), crimped ends toward the stove, three sheet metal screws per joint. Horizontal runs rise at least 1/4" per foot.

• Keep it as short and straight as possible, with the stove as close to the chimney as clearances allow. Extra length or elbows add draft resistance and creosote.
  • Secure every joint, including the flue collar, with three #10 x 1/2" sheet metal screws (holes pre-drilled in the collar).
  • A double wall connector reduces clearances. The manual's double wall figures are for Simpson DuraVent DVL; Metalbestos DS, Security, GSW and Ameritec are also acceptable.
  • Never pass through a floor, ceiling, attic or roof space, closet or similar concealed space. Through a combustible wall, conform to NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365 (pass-through systems A to D, p. 12) using a wall thimble or pass-through.
  • Connector clearances: Figure 5, p. 11. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct.
Connect to the chimney
A listed Type HT (2100° F) chimney per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved masonry chimney with a flue liner. 6" inside diameter for new installs; an existing 8" flue with a reducer.

• Size: not less than the flue collar, nor more than three times its cross-sectional area. Oversized flues build creosote.
  • Prefabricated: follow the chimney maker's instructions and buy the pass-through, tee, fire-stops, insulation shield, flashing and cap from the same maker. Choose an interior chimney whenever possible.
  • Masonry: have a professional check it for cracks, loose mortar, deterioration and blockage first; the cleanout door must seal tightly. Maximum 6" diameter or 8" x 8" tile. Brick or block at least 4" thick, or rubble or stone, must use a liner.
  • Liners: tile with at least 5/8" wall in refractory mortar with 1" air space; or UL listed 6" stainless, insulated or wrapped; or another listed liner meeting type HT.
  • Clearance: interior chimney at least 2" to combustibles (insulation at least 2" away, fire stops at floors and ceilings); exterior at least 1".
  • Height: at least 3 feet above the roof opening and 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet; recommended minimum 16 feet off the floor (top exit) or 19 feet (rear exit), maximum 30 feet.
Check the draft
Measure at installation: the stove needs 0.06" to 0.1" WC. Above 0.1" WC install a stovepipe damper; make sure the chimney is long enough for the minimum.
Mobile home (if applicable)
Install per 24 CFR Part 3280 (HUD) with the outside air kit, the stove fastened to the floor and a removable listed mobile home chimney kit. Never in a sleeping room.

• Outside air kit is required in all mobile home installations.
  • Permanently attach the stove to the floor with the shipping clips and fasteners long enough to reach the subfloor.
  • Mobile Home Chimney & Connector Kit to US/UL103 or CAN/ULC-S629, removable for transport: stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof, and the vapor barrier where the chimney penetrates.
  • Remove the chimney when transporting the home.
Break-in fires
The first fire, and the first of each season, is a small low fire: warm but not hot to the touch, then allowed to die out. Inspect the stovepipe and chimney afterward.

panels.title: Stove smokes or back-puffs
items: Operating technique → open the air fully a minute before opening the door, bypass open
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney, briefly open a window
Blocked, oversized, undersized or short chimney → check for blockage, reline, draft inducer, lengthen
Bypass not closed in the active range, or catalyst not working → close bypass, inspect catalyst
Extra low burn rate or chimney down-draft → burn hotter, install a chimney cap

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door, glass gasket leak → close tightly, replace gaskets
Excessive draft over 0.1" WC → stovepipe damper(s), operate at low burn
Extra long or oversized chimney → shorten or reline, add damper(s)
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Poor quality or green wood → air-dried at least one year, high Btu species
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate
Leaky stovepipe or chimney, excessive ash → check the installation, empty ash more often

panels.title: Catalyst problems
items: Fly ash build-up → light-off not reached, bypass closed too soon, or char-heavy fuel
Plugging or masking (soot, creosote) → wet or pitchy wood before light-off; an hour of hot burning may clear it
Warping or bowing → too hot for long periods; reduce the air setting

light.title: Building an everyday fire
light.html:
Every fire starts with the bypass open. You close it once the catalyst probe reads Active.

  1. Open the bypass handle (pointed toward the front of the stove), then open the front door.
  2. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Build a tee-pee of about 10 pieces of kindling over it, each 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long.
  3. Open the primary air control fully by sliding it all the way to the left.
  4. Light the paper under the kindling. Leave the door slightly ajar for a moment, until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull.
  5. Close the door and let the fire burn.
  6. Once the kindling is burning, open the door and add logs, small ones first. Keep them away from the glass so the air-wash system works properly.
  7. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst probe reads Active, close the bypass handle.
  8. Run it on a high setting for about 20 minutes so the catalyst stays active. Then set the burn rate with the primary air control.
New stove, or first fire of the season? Build a small break-in fire instead (see "Break in a new stove").
Keep the door closed while the stove is in use. Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

controls.title: Air control, bypass and catalyst probe
controls.html:
Primary air control

The lever sits under the ash lip. More air gives a faster, hotter burn; less air gives a slower burn with less heat. All the way left is the most air, all the way right the least. It never closes completely.

Bypass handle

Pointed toward the front of the stove, the bypass is open and smoke goes around the catalyst. Pointed toward the back, it is closed and smoke goes through the catalyst. Open it to start a fire and every time before you open the door. Close it once the catalyst is up to temperature.

Catalyst probe

  • Inactive: keep the bypass open until the stove heats up.
  • Active: close the bypass. The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F.
  • Too Hot: keep the door closed, close the air control fully, and let the stove cool until the probe is back in Active.
Note: pp. 21, 24 and 25 say to move the air lever left for more air and right for less; p. 24 also says to pull the handle toward you for a higher burn rate and push it toward the stove for a lower one.

breakin.title: Breaking in your stove
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned slowly. Firing a new stove too hard can crack the stone or damage other parts. Build this gentle fire for your first fire and the first fire of every season.

  1. Open the bypass handle and the front door. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox and crisscross about ten pieces of kindling over it (1/2" thick, 10" to 16" long).
  2. Open the primary air control fully, to the left stop.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly ajar until the kindling catches and the draft pulls, then close it.
  4. Keep a steady, low fire. The stove should get warm, not hot, to the touch. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  5. Once it is warm but not hot, close the primary air control fully and let the fire die out completely.
  6. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing mean the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells are normal

The first fires give off some smoke and fumes as the paints and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. Afterward, inspect the stovepipe and chimney and clean them if needed, because cool break-in fires can build creosote quickly.

reload.title: Reloading and burn rates
reload.html:
Reloading

  1. Open the bypass handle before you open the door.
  2. Open the door just a crack, pause so the firebox clears of smoke, then open it fully.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. Leave a small valley in the coals behind the lower primary air opening so the load relights faster.
  4. If the fire had cooled or burned down to charcoal, run it at a medium to high rate for about 10 minutes, until the catalyst reaches about 600 °F. Then close the bypass.

To keep creosote down, p. 30 also says to burn the stove with the primary air control fully open for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading. That gets the secondary combustion going early. The 10 minutes in step 4 is for bringing the catalyst up to about 600 °F so you can close the bypass.

Burn rates

  • Low: air control all the way right. Long periods on low build creosote, so check the venting often.
  • Medium: anywhere between. Experiment to find what suits your setup.
  • High: air all the way left, firebox fully loaded on hot coals. Run on high once or twice a day for 35 to 45 minutes to heat the stovepipe and chimney.
Don't over-fire. Signs include warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, and a discolored stovepipe. If you suspect it, stop using the stove and contact your dealer immediately. Over-firing voids the warranty.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural firewood (cordwood), in logs up to 18" long. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood generally burns cleaner and more efficiently than softwood or green wood.

Dry wood matters

  • Burn only dry, seasoned wood. Wet wood greatly reduces your efficiency and can greatly affect the stove's emissions.
  • Seasoned firewood is typically at or near 20% moisture. A hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Season green wood by splitting, stacking and air-drying it for a year. Green wood may give less than 2000 Btu per pound; dry wood up to 7000.
  • Stack it on skids or blocks, off the ground, and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Don't store firewood within the stove's clearances to combustibles.

Never burn

Garbage or trash, lawn clippings, coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, kiln-dried, painted or treated (including pressure-treated) wood, unseasoned (wet or green) wood, plywood, particleboard, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), driftwood (including salt water driftwood) and other previously salt water saturated materials, railroad ties, asphalt products, construction or demolition debris, waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners, solvents, manure or animal remains, flammable fluids, highly volatile fuel or other combustible material, or anything containing asbestos, plastic or rubber (including tires). Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective, cause smoke and damage the catalyst. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are allowed for lighting. Never use chemicals or flammable fluids to start a fire: they cause dangerous burning conditions in the stove. Keep all such materials away from the stove. Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space. At high levels, carbon dioxide could result in personal injury or death.

Don't load wood encrusted with ice into a burning stove. The thermal shock can cause damage.

ash.title: Removing and disposing of ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, or sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer of ash in the firebox if you prefer.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and remove only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Don't let ash build up around the door opening. It can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel and stop the door sealing.
  4. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Put nothing else in it, and don't pour water into it.
  5. Close the lid. Set the container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles.
Coals can stay hot for several days. Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, in trash cans with other trash, or in paper or plastic bags. Never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring. Keep the ashes in the closed container until all the coals have thoroughly cooled.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Only clean the glass when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. For the inside, dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the glass in a circular motion.
  2. When the deposits are gone, finish with window cleaner or a stove glass cleaner from your dealer. Use the same on the outside.
  3. Wipe the cleaner off with a soft cloth or black and white newsprint.
No razor blades, steel wool or abrasives. Scratches weaken the glass. Use only a cleaner made for wood stoves.

Glass that always stays dirty means you are burning too cool or your wood is wet. Keep logs away from the glass.

Broken or chipped glass

Don't use the stove until the glass is replaced. Use only the ceramic glass made for this stove: glass kit 90-58305, from your dealer.

The manual also prints 90-58300 as the glass kit on pp. 30 and 31; its parts list (p. 35) gives 90-58305 for the glass kit and 90-58300 for the gasket kit.
Note: p. 30 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass; p. 31 gives tips for replacing it yourself (work gloves, safety glasses).

upkeep.title: Upkeep checklist
upkeep.html:
Every week

  • Empty the ashes, sooner if the firebox is full.

Every other month

  • Look over the chimney connector and chimney for creosote.
  • Do the dollar bill test: with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing. Adjust the latch or change the gasket.
  • Check the face of the catalyst for fly ash and soot, and remove it with a soft-bristled brush. Look at it at least 3 times a heating season.

End of every season

  • Take apart and clean the chimney connector. Replace pieces showing rust or wear.
  • Inspect the chimney and clean it if needed. Clean out the inside of the stove.
  • Check and clean the catalyst if needed. Replace door gasket that is worn, frayed, cracked or extremely hard.

Creosote

Settle on a routine for your fuel, stove and firing technique. Check for creosote daily until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe. The hotter the fire, the less creosote is deposited, so weekly cleaning may be necessary in mild weather even though monthly cleaning may be enough in the coldest months. The every-other-month look above is the least the manual asks for. If creosote builds up, check monthly. Remove it once it is more than 1/4" thick; the manual recommends a certified chimney sweep, and a professional inspection before each heating season. Replace door gasket every two to three seasons.

safety.title: Safety and chimney fires
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while it burns. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away; touching it can burn skin.
  • Keep furniture, drapes, clothing and other things that burn at least 36" from the stove.
  • Never put clothing or candles on a hot stove, and never modify it.
  • Install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors throughout the home, including bedrooms and hallways, and test them.
  • Keep an "A B C" rated fire extinguisher handy.

If you have a chimney fire

  1. If it's too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away.
  2. Otherwise, close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if you have one.
  4. Close the bypass damper.
  5. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. The instant steam can cause serious harm. When the fire is out, leave the air control and bypass closed and let the stove die out. Inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney thoroughly and fix any damage before you use it again.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's limited warranty covers the original retail purchaser of a stove installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their representative. It isn't transferable and starts on the original invoice date. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles, latches; steel and firebox5 years
Electrical and gas components2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, all else1 year

In the first year Hearthstone pays for warranty labor by an authorized dealer, if a dealer installed the stove.

The catalyst

Its maker, Applied Ceramics, replaces it free if it stops working within two years, then at a prorated price ($130.00 in year 3 up to $160.00 in year 6).

Note: the catalyst warranty gives the free-replacement period as two (2) years, then says one replacement catalyst is given for each defective catalyst returned during "the three year period" (p. 37).

Not covered

  • Over-firing, or use not per the manual and codes
  • Wrong fuels, or unapproved parts or changes
  • Normal wear on paint, gaskets, baffles, refractory and glass

For a claim, contact your Hearthstone dealer. You can register online at hearthstonestoves.com or by mail; registering isn't required for coverage.

Insulation, windows, floor plan, placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. Not to be considered the home's primary heat source (p. 4).

conflicts.issue: Primary air direction: lever left = more air, right = less (pp. 21, 24 step 2, 25 low/high burn) vs 'pull the handle towards you for a higher burn rate, push towards the stove for a lower' (p. 24 step 8; break-in step 6 'pushing it fully inward toward the stove').
Run time after reloading: 'medium to high firing rate for about 10 minutes' to reach ~600 °F (p. 25) vs 'primary air control fully open for 15 to 20 minutes' after reloading (p. 30).
conflicts.reason: Different purposes that fit together: p. 25's 'about 10 minutes' at a medium to high rate is the time to bring the catalyst to about 600 °F before closing the bypass when rekindling a cool or charcoal-phase fire; p. 30's 15 to 20 minutes with the air fully open after reloading is a creosote-prevention practice. Running fully open for 15 to 20 minutes also meets the medium-to-high run, so both are shown as written.

conflicts.issue: Glass kit part number: 'Required Glass Kit: Part Number: 90-58300' (pp. 30, 31) vs parts list 90-58300 = GASKET KIT, 90-58305 = GLASS KIT (p. 35).
Who replaces the glass: 'Only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel' (p. 30) vs 'If you replace the glass yourself, wear work gloves and safety glasses' (p. 31).
Emission rate unit: 'certified at 0.98 gr/hr.' (p. 2) vs 'Emissions: 0.98 g/hr.' (p. 7).
Catalyst warranty free-replacement window: 'ceases to function with two (2) years' vs 'one replacement catalyst for each defective catalyst returned during the three year period' (same page).

Creosote check frequency: 'Check daily for creosote build-up until experience shows how often you need to clean to be safe' (p. 6) vs 'inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months', and 'at least monthly' if creosote builds up (pp. 5, 30).
conflicts.reason: The daily check is the routine to follow until experience shows how often you need to clean (p. 6); the every-two-months and monthly inspections are stated minimums ('at least', p. 30). Both are shown as written.
